meta.title: Who really said "The key is not to prioritize what's on your schedule, but to schedule your priorities"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Covey — verified word for word in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), Habit 3. Often mis-filed under his later First Things First.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The key is not to prioritize what's on your schedule, but to schedule your priorities'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: the line is Stephen Covey's own, from The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), Habit 3 — not First Things First, where it's usually filed.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and word for word. The sentence appears in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (New York: Simon & Schuster, 1989) in the Habit 3 chapter, “Put First Things First,” where Covey lists what a weekly planning tool has to do. Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ places it at p. 161 of that edition; the passage itself is easy to check against the book’s text.

source.excerpt: The key is not to prioritize what’s on your schedule, but to schedule your priorities.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ files the line under The Seven Habits Of Highly Effective People (1989) and gives p. 161 — not under “Attributed” or “Misattributed,” where several other Covey-credited lines sit.

Checked against the book itself: the sentence appears word for word in the Habit 3 chapter, inside the “Quadrant II Focus” criterion where Covey argues for weekly rather than daily planning (full text at the Internet Archive ↗).

The Internet Archive catalogue record ↗ for the first Fireside edition confirms Simon and Schuster, New York, 1989, ISBN 0671663984. Pagination shifts between printings and formats, so treat p. 161 as specific to the 1989 edition rather than universal.
Quote Investigator ↗ has no article on this line, and no earlier or rival claimant turned up in searching — the attribution itself has never been contested.
source.excerptNote: Quoted in brief because the book is in copyright. In the surrounding passage Covey is setting out six things a planning tool must do; under the third, “Quadrant II Focus,” he argues that organising the week beats organising the day, because day-level tools can only rank crises and busywork — and this sentence is the conclusion he draws from it.

author.name: Stephen Covey
author.heading: About Stephen R. Covey
author.bio: Stephen Richards Covey was born in Salt Lake City in 1932 and died in Idaho Falls in 2012. He taught business at Brigham Young University before The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989) made him one of the most-read management writers alive — Time named him one of the 25 most influential Americans in 1996. He returned to the time-management argument in First Things First (1994) and The 8th Habit (2004).

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The name on this quote is right. Almost everything else that travels with it — the book, and often the wording — is not.

items.why: Quote collections routinely file the line under Covey’s later time-management book; Shortform’s “First Things First quotes” roundup ↗ lists it there. The sentence is documented in the earlier 7 Habits (1989), in the Habit 3 chapter.

items.who: “The key is not to prioritize your schedule, but to schedule your priorities”
items.why: A shortened form drops “what’s on” and circulates as if it were the original — this 2013 post ↗ builds a whole essay on the trimmed version, credits Covey, and names no book at all.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording is genuinely Covey’s: it appears verbatim in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), in Habit 3, “Put First Things First” — where Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ also places it, at p. 161 of that edition.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Covey wrote the line as the hinge of Habit 3. His complaint about the planners of the day was that they let you rank an already-crowded morning — useful, but it only sorts crises and busywork. His fix was to plan the week rather than the day, and to drop the things that actually matter into the calendar while it is still empty, so everything else has to arrange itself around them.

The sentence is a chiasmus: two nouns, schedule and priorities, swapped around the verb. That symmetry is exactly why it detached from the book so cleanly and now turns up on slides, mugs and LinkedIn posts with no source attached — and why it gets quietly reworded in transit.
context.detailsSummary: Why the wrong book keeps getting the credit
detailsBody: Covey came back to the same ground in 1994, five years on, with First Things First — a whole book built on the Quadrant II idea that Habit 3 introduced. Because that later title is the one people think of as “the Covey time-management book,” quote collections file this sentence there. The line itself sits in the earlier work.

A practical caution for anyone citing it: page numbers move. Wikiquote’s p. 161 belongs to the 1989 edition, and the book has been reset for the Fireside, 25th- and 30th-anniversary printings. Cite the chapter — Habit 3 — and the page number becomes optional rather than wrong.
context.pull: Same two words, reversed — and the calendar stops being the boss.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section lists "The key is not to prioritize what's on your schedule, but to schedule your priorities" under The Seven Habits Of Highly Effective People (1989) at p. 161.

The sentence appears verbatim in the text of The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, in the Habit 3 "Put First Things First" chapter, within the "Quadrant II Focus" criterion, immediately after the sentence about third-generation planning tools organising crises and busywork.
The Internet Archive catalogue record gives Simon and Schuster, New York, 1989, first Fireside edition, ISBN 0671663984, 366 pages, borrowable scan.
Wikipedia gives 1989 as the first publication date of The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People and names Habit 3 as "Put First Things First," with the urgent/important quadrant framework.

Wikipedia gives Stephen Richards Covey's dates as born 24 October 1932 in Salt Lake City and died 16 July 2012 in Idaho Falls, describes him as an American educator, author, businessman and motivational speaker, lists The 7 Habits (1989) and First Things First (1994), and notes Time naming him one of the 25 most influential people in 1996.
Shortform's "First Things First Quotes" page lists this quote among quotes presented as coming from the book First Things First.
This post reproduces the shortened variant "The key is not to prioritize your schedule, but to schedule your priorities," credits it to Stephen Covey, and names no book or source.
FranklinCovey's official book page for The 7 Habits lists Habit 3 as "Put First Things First — Prioritize and achieve your most important goals instead of constantly reacting to urgencies."
A Quote Investigator site search for "schedule your priorities" returns no article investigating this quote.
